title: Faulty Keyboard
description:
# Faulty Keyboard

Your laptop keyboard has one fault: whenever you type the character `'i'`, the text already on the screen is reversed, and that `'i'` is **not** inserted into the text.

You are given the exact string `s` that you type from left to right. Return the final string shown on the screen after every character has been processed.

The screen starts empty. Each other character is appended to the text; typing `i` only reverses the existing text.

## Example 1:

**Input:** s = "string"
**Output:** "rtsng"
**Explanation:** The characters `s`, `t`, and `r` are typed normally, so the screen shows "str". Typing `i` reverses it to "rts". Then `n` and `g` are appended, giving "rtsng".

## Example 2:

**Input:** s = "poiinter"
**Output:** "ponter"
**Explanation:** After typing `p` and `o`, the first `i` reverses "po" to "op". The second `i` reverses it back to "po". The remaining characters append normally.

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= s.length <= 100`
*   `s` consists only of lowercase English letters.
*   `s[0] != 'i'`

solutions.name: StringBuilder Direct Reverse
solutions.description:
## Approach

Simulate the keyboard exactly. Append every normal character to a `StringBuilder`; when the faulty key `i` appears, call `reverse()` on the builder and do not append the `i`.

## Key Insight

This route is the clearest statement-level baseline: it directly models the screen. Its weakness is that many reversals can repeatedly move the same characters.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n^2) in the worst case because each `reverse()` may scan the current screen.
- Space Complexity: O(n) for the builder holding the screen contents.

solutions.name: Deque Direction Simulation
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep a deque of characters and a boolean that tells whether the logical screen is currently reversed. Normal characters go to the back in normal mode and to the front in reversed mode. The final read direction depends on the boolean.

## Key Insight

A reversal only changes which end is considered the front. By toggling a direction flag instead of moving all characters, each typed character is inserted once.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n), since every input character is handled once and every output character is read once.
- Space Complexity: O(n) for the deque and answer builder.

solutions.name: Two Buffer Direction Merge
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store characters typed during reversed phases in a front buffer and characters typed during normal phases in a back buffer. At the end, reverse only the buffer whose order must be flipped and concatenate the two parts.

## Key Insight

The final string can be described by where characters were typed relative to the current direction. Delaying the actual reversal turns repeated screen reversals into one final merge.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n), because each character is appended once and each buffer is reversed at most once.
- Space Complexity: O(n) for the two buffers.

solutions.name: Run Deque Deferred Reversal
solutions.description:
## Approach

Group consecutive non-`i` characters into runs. When a run ends, place it at the back in normal mode or place its reversed form at the front in reversed mode. If the final mode is reversed, read the stored runs from back to front and reverse each run while reading.

## Key Insight

This is the deque idea lifted from individual characters to whole runs. It teaches that the operation is about orientation, so contiguous typed text can be moved as a block.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n), since every character joins one run and is copied a constant number of times.
- Space Complexity: O(n) for the stored runs and final answer.

tests.description: sample with two adjacent reversal triggers
no faulty key leaves the string unchanged
a trailing reversal on one character keeps the same screen
a normal character after a reversal appends to the logical end
multiple separated reversals interleave with normal characters
two reversals create a front block before later appends
two trailing reversals cancel each other
a final reversal flips a longer accumulated screen
alternating single-character runs should not emit any i characters
a final reversal after a reversed run checks both order and placement
